paragraphs.title: Writing the Scroll and the Prophecy to Baruch

easy.explanation: The verse says that Baruch the son of Neriah wrote the words in a book.
easy.q: Who wrote Jeremiah’s words in a book?

easy.explanation: Baruch wrote the words at the mouth of Jeremiah.
easy.q: From whose mouth did Baruch write the words?

easy.explanation: The verse identifies the time as the fourth year of Jehoiakim.
easy.q: In what year of Jehoiakim did this occur?

answers: He dictated the words to Baruch
medium.explanation: Baruch wrote the words from Jeremiah’s dictation.
medium.q: What was Jeremiah’s role in the writing of the book?

answers: The time when Baruch completed the writing
The time when Jehoiakim became king
The time when Jeremiah left Judah
medium.explanation: The phrase refers to Baruch’s writing of Jeremiah’s words in a book.
medium.q: What does the phrase “when he had written these words in a book” describe?

medium.explanation: The prophecy is spoken unto Baruch the son of Neriah.
medium.q: Which person is specifically addressed by the prophecy in this chapter?

answers: Jeremiah copied what Baruch had written
challenge.explanation: The phrase indicates that Baruch recorded Jeremiah’s spoken words.
challenge.q: What does the phrase “at the mouth of Jeremiah” most clearly mean?

answers: Baruch wrote Jeremiah’s words, the scroll was destroyed, and a new book was written
Jehoiakim wrote the book, Baruch became king, and Jeremiah stopped speaking
Baruch became king, Jeremiah burned the book, and Jehoiakim wrote a prophecy
challenge.explanation: The wider account includes Baruch’s writing, the burning of the scroll, and the writing of another book.
challenge.q: Which sequence best fits the idea connected with this passage?

answers: It places the writing at a specific point in Judah’s history
It shows that Baruch was older than Jeremiah
It identifies the year when Baruch became king
challenge.explanation: The date places the writing within the reign and historical setting of Jehoiakim.
challenge.q: Why is the date in the fourth year of Jehoiakim important?

easy.explanation: The verse begins, “Thus saith the Lord, the God of Israel, unto thee, O Baruch.”
easy.q: Who speaks to Baruch in verse 2?
What does Baruch say at the beginning of his complaint?

medium.explanation: Baruch says, “the Lord hath added grief to my sorrow.”
medium.q: What had the Lord added to Baruch’s sorrow?

answers: He fainted in his sighing and found no rest
He rejoiced in his strength and found peace
He slept after his labor and forgot his sorrow
medium.explanation: The verse says that Baruch fainted in his sighing and found no rest.
medium.q: How does Baruch describe his condition?

medium.explanation: “Grief” refers to the sorrow added to Baruch’s suffering.
medium.q: What does the word “grief” mean in this context?

answers: It was both emotional and ongoing
It was only a brief moment of happiness
It came from becoming a king
challenge.explanation: His woe, sighing, faintness, and lack of rest show continuing distress.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from Baruch’s words about his distress?

answers: It shows that his sorrow had exhausted him
It shows that he had won a victory
It shows that he was preparing to travel
challenge.explanation: The wording presents sorrow so intense that it left him weak and weary.
challenge.q: How does the wording “I fainted in my sighing” strengthen the description of Baruch’s condition?

answers: Woe, grief, sighing, and no rest
challenge.explanation: These words express the main elements of Baruch’s complaint in the passage.
challenge.q: Which group of words best summarizes Baruch’s complaint?

easy.explanation: The Lord says, “that which I have built will I break down.”
easy.q: What does the Lord say He will break down?

easy.explanation: He is told, “seek them not,” referring to great things for himself.
easy.q: What is Baruch told not to seek?

easy.explanation: The Lord says, “thy life will I give unto thee for a prey.”
easy.q: What does the Lord promise to give Baruch?

answers: Both describe the Lord’s judgment and destruction
Both describe the writing of the book
medium.explanation: The two expressions describe the destruction of what the Lord had built and planted.
medium.q: What is the relationship between breaking down and plucking up in this passage?

answers: The Lord was bringing evil upon all flesh
There was no longer anything to write
medium.explanation: The Lord says that evil would come upon all flesh, so Baruch was not to pursue personal greatness.
medium.q: Why should Baruch not seek great things for himself?

answers: Something preserved or rescued from danger
medium.explanation: The expression means that Baruch’s life would be spared or preserved.
medium.q: In the phrase “for a prey,” what does “prey” mean?

answers: The land would suffer destruction, but Baruch’s life would be preserved
Baruch would be destroyed before the land
There would be no judgment at all
challenge.explanation: The passage announces widespread judgment while promising to preserve Baruch’s life.
challenge.q: What contrast appears between the judgment on the land and the promise to Baruch?

answers: It applies wherever Baruch may go
It requires Baruch to remain in one place
It promises Baruch a new kingdom
challenge.explanation: The wording extends the promise to every place where Baruch goes.
challenge.q: What does “in all places whither thou goest” suggest about the promise to Baruch?

answers: Destruction of what was built and planted, a warning not to seek greatness, and preservation of Baruch’s life
A promise of riches, the rebuilding of the land, and a command to seek greatness
Preservation of the land, the crowning of Baruch, and a promise of peace
challenge.explanation: The verses move from judgment, to the warning against seeking greatness, to the promise of preserved life.
challenge.q: Which order best represents the ideas in verses 4–5?
